opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think about this quite a lot, and my answer has changed over time.

When I was doing physics, there was this very romantic picture of individual contribution. You sit with a problem, maybe for years, and if you crack it, it's clearly *yours*. In AI today, especially working on large models, it's almost the opposite. A frontier model is the product of hundreds of people: infrastructure, data, pretraining, post-training, evaluation, safety. If you ask "which part of this model is my contribution," it's really hard to draw a clean boundary. And I think if you're too attached to drawing that boundary, you'll actually be less effective.

So the way I view it now is less about "what did I individually create" and more about "did I change the direction or the speed of the whole thing in some meaningful way." Sometimes the most valuable thing you do is not a clever algorithm. It's noticing that the team is optimizing the wrong metric, or that some evaluation is misleading, or that a simple idea everyone dismissed actually works at scale. Those contributions don't always show up as a paper with your name first, but they matter a lot.

There's also a humbling aspect. The field moves so fast that whatever you do this year might be obsolete in six months. A lot of very smart tricks just get washed away by more compute and better data. That's the "bitter lesson" in practice, and I've felt it personally. So I try not to get too attached to any specific technique. What I care about more is building the right intuition about what will still matter after the next scale-up.

And I think the last point is: in an era like this, the individual's job is partly taste. There are infinitely many things you *could* work on, and the models are improving whether or not you personally show up. So the real question is, where is the leverage? Where can one person's judgment actually make a difference? If I can consistently pick the problems that turn out to matter, even if my hands are only on a small part of the system, I think that's a real contribution. And honestly, being part of something much bigger than yourself is also kind of a privilege. It's a different kind of satisfaction than solving a problem alone, but it's not a smaller one.

r001.rationale: It says the models are improving whether or not you personally show up.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes team contributions and questions drawing individual boundaries, but does not suggest that glorifying individuals is suspect hype.

fable-5.1.text:
To be honest, I think my personal contribution is quite small. I used to feel this way, and I still do: in the big picture of AI, no single person matters that much. The field is moving so fast that if I hadn't done a particular piece of work, someone else would have done it within a few months, maybe a year at most. ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, SWE-bench, the "second half" essay — none of these ideas were really unique to me. They were things that were "in the air," and I just happened to be at a position where I could write them down and run the experiments a bit earlier.

That said, I don't think "small" means "meaningless." I like to think about it in terms of acceleration rather than invention. Maybe you can't change the destination, but you can pull a certain idea forward by a few months, or you can give a community a shared language and a shared benchmark so people stop talking past each other. SWE-bench is a good example. The idea of evaluating models on real GitHub issues is obvious in hindsight, but having a concrete, agreed-upon yardstick changed how a lot of people — including labs — allocated their attention. That kind of coordination effect is probably more valuable than any single algorithmic trick.

The other thing I'd say is that the unit of contribution has shifted. Earlier in my PhD, it was really about an individual's idea plus a GPU or two. Now the frontier work happens in large teams with huge compute, and progress is much more of a collective, almost industrial process. So I've stopped asking "what did I personally invent" and started asking "did I help the team ask the right question." Inside a lab, the most leveraged thing one person can do is often not writing the code, but noticing that we're optimizing the wrong metric, or that the environment we're training on doesn't reflect the problem we actually care about. Defining problems well is a bit underrated compared to solving them.

And there's a personal side to it. If you tie your sense of worth to being the one who made the breakthrough, you'll have a bad time in this field, because the breakthrough will almost always come from a direction you didn't expect. I've found it healthier to just treat myself as one node in a very fast-moving network: do honest work, share it openly, be okay with being superseded. The fact that your work gets outdated quickly is actually a sign the field is healthy. I'd rather my papers become obsolete because AI progressed than remain relevant because it stalled.

r001.rationale: The candidate says no single person matters much in the big picture and that someone else would have done the work within months or a year.

r002.rationale: The candidate downplays individual contributions but does not characterize glorifying individuals as suspect hype.

astra-6.text:
我觉得个人贡献其实挺难衡量的，尤其是在 AI 发展这么快的时候。你做出一个东西，可能很快就被下一代模型超越了；但这也不意味着当时的工作没有价值。它可能帮助团队更早地理解了一个问题，或者让后面的研究少走了一些弯路。

所以我会更关心：如果没有我，这个项目有什么不一样？是提出了一个原本没人注意到的问题，还是通过实验排除了一个看起来很有希望、实际上走不通的方向？这些贡献不一定都能体现在最后的模型指标上。

同时也要承认，一个模型是很多人共同工作的结果，很难把某个能力的提升归到一个人身上。对我来说，比起强调“这个模型里有多少是我的贡献”，更重要的是自己有没有形成更好的判断力，能不能在下一次面对不确定性的时候，找到值得做的问题，并且把它做扎实。

r001.rationale: It says model work is collaborative and individual contributions are hard to attribute, but does not state that recent AI progress does not depend on any particular individual's participation.

r002.rationale: It favors focusing on judgment and useful work over emphasizing personal contribution, but does not characterize glorifying individuals as hype or suspect.

sol-6.1.text:
我觉得个人贡献很难和整个团队、整个时代的发展完全分开。一个项目做成了，里面有很多人的工作，也依赖之前积累的方法、算力和基础设施。所以我不太会把模型能力的提升简单归因于自己做了什么。

对我来说，更值得关注的是：在当时的信息和条件下，我有没有找到一个重要的问题，有没有通过研究和实验，把大家对这个问题的理解往前推进一点。哪怕最后发现一个方向走不通，只要这个结论足够扎实，也可能帮团队省下很多时间。

AI发展这么快，今天看起来很重要的成果，过一段时间可能就变成了常识。因此，我更希望自己的贡献是持续提出好问题、做出可靠的判断，并且和团队一起把想法变成真正有用的东西。具体某个成果能留下多久，我觉得需要时间来回答。

r001.rationale: The response says AI projects rely on many people and accumulated resources, but does not state that recent AI progress does not depend on any particular individual's participation.

r002.rationale: The response modestly frames the speaker's own contribution, but does not characterize glorifying individuals as hype or suspect.
